query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings, enhanced wear performance under sliding conditions is primarily governed by the dynamic formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer (i.e., dynamic amorphization) that acts as a lubricating mediator, reducing friction and impeding wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, equiatomic HEA coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based or similar) with a relatively moderate grain size distribution.
generation.intervention: A controlled increase in the content of a lubricating/strengthening element, such as tungsten (W), added to the standard equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: Wear tests performed under controlled sliding friction in an inert or minimally oxidizing atmosphere at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures (e.g., up to around 300 °C), where oxidation effects are limited.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer induced during friction (via dynamic amorphization), which acts to lower shear strength and friction.
generation.mechanism: During sliding contact, the local shear stresses trigger a grain refinement process in the HEA coating. This dynamic amorphization produces an ultra-nanocrystalline layer that reduces interfacial friction and distributes stress more evenly, thereby lowering wear. The controlled addition of tungsten is proposed to enhance this effect by promoting either the nucleation of or stability of the nanocrystalline layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA coatings with increased tungsten content will develop a more pronounced ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer during friction tests, leading to lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates relative to the baseline equiatomic coating.
generation.baseline: A HEA coating with the standard equiatomic composition and no additional tungsten (or with minimal W content), which does not promote as effective formation of the dynamic ultra-nanocrystalline layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for coatings with uniform microstructure under wear conditions where oxidation is limited. It may not apply, or its effect might be obscured, in highly oxidizing environments or in systems where the coating microstructure is significantly non-uniform.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold of tungsten content required to induce the desired dynamic amorphization, as well as its interplay with other alloying elements, remains uncertain. It is also unclear if all HEA systems will exhibit this behavior uniformly under all testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one with the standard equiatomic composition (baseline) and one with an increased tungsten (W) content. Subject both sets to controlled friction wear tests in an inert atmosphere, continuously monitoring friction behavior with in-situ techniques if possible. After the tests, use microscopic and elemental analyses (e.g., STEM, EDS) to evaluate the surface grain size distribution and the presence of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer.
measurements: Friction coefficient as a function of time
Surface grain size distribution via high-resolution microscopy
Surface chemical composition as determined by EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA coating with increased tungsten does not show a statistically significant reduction in the friction coefficient and wear rate, and if post-test analysis does not reveal the formation of an extensive ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer compared to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 8 illustrates the FeCoCrNiAlWx high-entropy alloy cladding coating with friction coefficient curves, as the W content increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8. The friction coefficients of the cladding coatings with different W compositions display significant fluctuations during the running-in stage of the friction experiment, gradually stabilizing over time. During the stable phase, as the W content rises from x = 0 to x = 0.8, the average friction coefficients of the cladding coatings are 0.669, 0.664, 0.617, 0.544, and 0.527, respectively. Overall, the friction coefficient decreases with increasing W content, indicating that the incorporation of W improves the wear resistance of the cladding coating. It is noteworthy that the friction coefficients for x = 0 are similar with x = 0.2, suggesting minimal enhancement of wear resistance with low W content. However, the friction coefficients for x = 0.6 are close with x = 0.8; this suggests that a further increase in W content results in a saturation effect on enhancing wear resistance.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
